items.prompt: How does this unit define an "entry point"?
choices: The last function called before a response is returned
The first piece of code a given kind of request or event reaches — a route handler, event listener, CLI handler, or queue consumer
The main() function of the entire application
Any function with more than 10 lines of code
items.reference:
🚪 Entry point — first code a request reaches
📍 Examples: route handler, event listener, CLI command, queue consumer

Why: Finding it narrows down where to even start looking in an unfamiliar codebase.
items.explanation: An entry point is the first piece of code a specific kind of request or event reaches — for an HTTP API this is usually a route handler. Finding it is the first narrowing step before tracing anything further.

items.reference:
🚪 Entry point — first code a request reaches
📍 Examples: route handler, event listener, CLI command, queue consumer

Why: Finding it narrows down where to even start looking in an unfamiliar codebase.
items.explanation: The route registration (mapping the HTTP path and method to a controller function) is the entry point — it's the first place the specific request in question reaches inside the codebase.

items.prompt: What does "tracing execution" mean, per this unit?

items.reference:
🔗 Tracing execution — follow ONE concrete request through the real call sequence
🎯 Not a general survey of the whole codebase
items.explanation: Tracing execution means following one specific, concrete request through the real chain of function calls it triggers — not a general survey of the whole codebase or every possible path through it.

items.prompt: In the discount-bug scenario, tracing execution followed which chain of layers?
choices: Model → route → test

Service → route → model
items.reference:

🎯 Not a general survey of the whole codebase

items.prompt: Why does this unit recommend reading tests before diving into implementation code?
choices: Because tests are always shorter than implementation code
Because tests document intended behavior more reliably than comments (which can go stale) and more concretely than prose docstrings
Because implementation code is never worth reading

✅ More reliable than comments, more concrete than docstrings
items.explanation: Tests document intended behavior through concrete, checkable examples — more reliable than a comment (which can go stale without anyone noticing) and more concrete than a prose docstring.

items.prompt: Besides telling you what the code is supposed to do, what else does reading an existing test reveal?
choices: Nothing else — tests only describe expected outputs
The codebase's established pattern for handling similar cases (e.g. throwing an Error with a specific message), useful for writing a fix that matches the rest of the file
The exact salary of whoever wrote the test
Whether the code has ever been deployed to production
items.reference:
📖 Reading tests first — tests as documentation of intent
✅ More reliable than comments, more concrete than docstrings
items.explanation: Reading an existing test also reveals the codebase's established pattern for handling similar situations — like throwing an Error with a specific message — which is worth matching when writing a new fix so it fits the rest of the file.

items.prompt: What is a "call graph", as this unit defines it?

items.explanation: A call graph is the actual chain of function calls a request triggers as it executes — distinct from the folder structure, which organizes code by category rather than by execution order.

items.prompt: Why does this unit emphasize that a call graph "often doesn't match" folder structure?
choices: Because folder structure and execution order are actually always identical
Because folders group code by category (routes, services, models) while execution order depends on what calls what, which can jump across folders in any order
Because folders are randomly named and have no meaning
Because call graphs only apply to compiled languages
items.reference:
🕸️ Call graph — the real chain of function calls
📁 Often doesn't match the folder structure at all
items.explanation: Folders organize code by category or layer, while the call graph follows execution order — a request can jump from a `routes/` file to a `controllers/` file to a `services/` file, an order that has nothing to do with alphabetical or folder-based organization.

items.prompt: Implement `applyDiscount(order, code)` using the fixed rates in `discountCodes` (SAVE10 = 0.1, SAVE20 = 0.2). It should throw "Unknown discount code" for a code not in the map, throw "Discount already applied" if `order.appliedDiscounts` already contains the code, and otherwise push the code onto `order.appliedDiscounts` and reduce `order.total` by the rate.

tests.description: rejects applying the same code twice
tests.expr: (() => { const order = { total: 100, appliedDiscounts: [] }; applyDiscount(order, 'SAVE10'); let threw = false; try { applyDiscount(order, 'SAVE10'); } catch (e) { threw = true; } return expect(threw).toBe(true); })()

tests.description: leaves total unchanged after a rejected duplicate
tests.expr: (() => { const order = { total: 100, appliedDiscounts: [] }; applyDiscount(order, 'SAVE10'); try { applyDiscount(order, 'SAVE10'); } catch (e) {} return expect(order.total).toBe(90); })()

items.explanation: The fix checks for an unknown code first, then checks whether the code is already in `appliedDiscounts` before mutating anything — following the exact validate-before-mutate, throw-with-message pattern the existing tests in L3 already established, rather than inventing a different error-handling style.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Check unknown code → throw
2️⃣ Check duplicate code → throw
3️⃣ Only then mutate: push code, reduce total

Why: Matching the codebase's existing validate-before-mutate pattern (from the tests) keeps the fix consistent with the rest of the file.
